title: Tom Thumb
paragraphs: One night a poor woodcutter was sitting in his cottage by the fire, smoking his pipe, while his wife sat beside him spinning. “How lonely it is, wife,” he said, blowing out a long curl of smoke, “for the two of us to sit here by ourselves, with no children running around to keep us entertained, while everyone else seems so happy and cheerful with theirs!” “That is perfectly true,” said his wife with a sigh, turning her wheel. “How happy I would be if I had just one child! Even if it were tiny—even if it were no bigger than my thumb—I would be very happy, and I would love it dearly.” Now, strange as it may sound, this good woman’s wish came true in exactly the way she had put it. Not long afterward she had a little boy who was perfectly healthy and strong, but hardly bigger than my thumb. So they said, “Well, we can’t claim we didn’t get what we wished for, and small as he is, we will love him dearly.” And they named him Thomas Thumb.

They fed him plenty, but whatever they did he never grew any bigger. He stayed exactly the size he had been when he was born. Still, his eyes were bright and sharp, and he soon proved to be a clever little fellow who always knew what he was doing.

One day the woodcutter was getting ready to go into the forest to cut firewood. “I wish I had someone to bring the cart along after me,” he said, “because I’m in a hurry.” “Oh, father,” cried Tom, “I’ll take care of that. The cart will be in the forest by the time you need it.” The woodcutter laughed. “How could that be?” he said. “You can’t even reach the horse’s bridle.” “Never mind that, father,” said Tom. “If Mother will just harness the horse, I’ll climb into his ear and tell him which way to go.” “Well,” said his father, “let’s try it once.”

When the time came, his mother harnessed the horse to the cart and put Tom in its ear. Sitting there, the little man told the animal where to go, calling “Giddy-up!” and “Whoa!” as he needed, and the horse went along just as well as if the woodcutter had driven it into the forest himself. It happened that the horse was going a bit too fast and Tom was shouting, “Easy! Easy!” when two strangers came along. “How strange!” said one. “There’s a cart rolling along and I can hear a driver talking to the horse, but I can’t see anyone.” “That is odd,” said the other. “Let’s follow the cart and see where it goes.” So they followed it into the forest until they reached the spot where the woodcutter was. Tom Thumb saw his father and called out, “Look, father, here I am with the cart, safe and sound! Now lift me down!” His father held the horse with one hand and with the other lifted his son out of the horse’s ear and set him on a piece of straw, where he sat as cheerful as could be.

All this time the two strangers had been watching, too amazed to speak. Finally one drew the other aside and said, “That little rascal could make our fortune if we got hold of him and took him from town to town as a show. We should buy him.” So they went up to the woodcutter and asked what he wanted for the little man. “He’ll be better off with us than with you,” they said. “I won’t sell him at all,” said the father. “My own flesh and blood is worth more to me than all the silver and gold in the world.” But Tom heard what kind of deal they were after, and he crept up his father’s coat to his shoulder and whispered in his ear, “Take the money, father, and let them have me. I’ll be back with you soon enough.”

In the end the woodcutter agreed to sell Tom to the strangers for a big piece of gold, and they paid the price. “Where would you like to sit?” one of them asked. “Oh, put me on the brim of your hat. That will make a fine balcony for me. I can walk around there and see the countryside as we go.” They did as he asked, and once Tom had said goodbye to his father, they took him away with them.

They traveled on until it began to get dark, and then the little man said, “Let me down, I’m tired.” The man took off his hat and set him on a clod of earth in a plowed field beside the road. But Tom ran about among the furrows and finally slipped into an old mouse hole. “Good night, gentlemen!” he said. “I’m off! Watch me more carefully next time.” They rushed over and poked the ends of their sticks into the mouse hole, but it was no use. Tom only crawled farther and farther in, and soon it was completely dark, so they had to go on their way without their prize, as sulky as could be.

When Tom was sure they had gone, he came out of his hiding place. “How dangerous it is to walk in this plowed field!” he said. “If I fell off one of these huge clods, I would certainly break my neck.” By good luck he finally found a large empty snail shell. “That’s lucky,” he said. “I can sleep here quite comfortably.” And in he crept.

He was just dropping off to sleep when he heard two men go by, chatting. One of them said to the other, “How can we rob that rich parson’s house of its silver and gold?” “I’ll tell you!” cried Tom. “What was that noise?” said the thief, startled. “I’m sure I heard someone speak.” They stood still and listened, and Tom said, “Take me with you, and I’ll soon show you how to get the parson’s money.” “But where are you?” they asked. “Look around on the ground,” he answered, “and listen for where the voice comes from.” At last the thieves found him and picked him up in their hands. “You little rascal!” they said. “What could you do for us?” “Why, I can squeeze between the iron bars of the parson’s window and throw out to you whatever you want.” “Good idea,” said the thieves. “Come along, and we’ll see what you can do.”

When they reached the parson’s house, Tom slipped between the window bars into the room and then shouted at the top of his lungs, “Do you want everything that’s in here?” The thieves were terrified and said, “Quietly, quietly! Speak softly, so you don’t wake anyone.” But Tom acted as if he didn’t understand and bellowed again, “How much do you want? Shall I throw it all out?” The cook was lying in the next room, and hearing the noise she sat up in bed and listened. Meanwhile the thieves, frightened, had run off a short distance, but at last they got their nerve back and said, “The little rascal is only trying to make fools of us.” So they came back and whispered to him, “Now, no more of your cheeky jokes. Just throw us out some of the money.” Then Tom shouted as loudly as he could, “All right! Hold out your hands! Here it comes.”

The cook heard this quite clearly, so she jumped out of bed and ran to open the door. The thieves bolted as if a wolf were at their heels. The maid groped around, found nothing, and went off to fetch a light. By the time she came back, Tom had slipped away into the barn. She looked in every hole and corner and found nobody, so she went back to bed, thinking she must have been dreaming with her eyes open.

The little man crawled around the hayloft and finally found a cozy spot to finish his night’s rest. He lay down, meaning to sleep until daylight and then find his way home to his father and mother. But alas, how dreadfully things went wrong for him! What troubles and sorrows we all meet in this world! The cook got up early, before daybreak, to feed the cows. She went straight to the hayloft and carried off a large bundle of hay with the little man in the middle of it, fast asleep. He kept on sleeping and did not wake until he found himself in the cow’s mouth, for the cook had put the hay in the cow’s rack and the cow had picked Tom up in one mouthful. “Good heavens!” he said. “How did I end up in the mill?” But he soon realized where he really was, and he had to keep all his wits about him so that he would not get between the cow’s teeth and be crushed to death. At last down he went into her stomach. “It’s rather dark,” he said. “They forgot to put windows in this room to let the sun in. A candle wouldn’t be a bad idea.”

He made the best of his bad luck, but he did not like it in there one bit. Worst of all, hay kept tumbling down in ever greater amounts, and the room left for him shrank and shrank. Finally he yelled at the top of his voice, “Don’t bring me any more hay! Don’t bring me any more hay!”

The maid was milking the cow at that very moment. She heard someone speak but could see nobody, and she was sure it was the same voice she had heard in the night. She was so terrified that she toppled off her stool and spilled the milk-pail. Once she had scrambled up out of the dirt, she raced to her master the parson and cried, “Sir, sir, the cow is talking!” “Woman, you must be out of your mind!” said the parson. All the same, he went with her to the cow-house to find out what was going on.

They had barely stepped through the doorway when Tom shouted, “Don’t bring me any more hay!” Now the parson was frightened too. He decided the cow must be bewitched and ordered his man to kill her right then and there. So the cow was slaughtered and cut open, and the stomach with Tom inside it was tossed onto a dunghill.

Tom set about trying to get free, which was no easy job. He had just managed to push his head out when more bad luck struck. A hungry wolf leapt up and gulped down the whole stomach, Tom and all, in a single swallow, then ran off.

Even so, Tom did not lose heart. It occurred to him that the wolf might enjoy a bit of conversation on the way, so he called out, “My good friend, I can show you a wonderful feast.” “Where?” asked the wolf. “At such and such a house,” said Tom, describing his own father’s house. “You can squeeze through the drain into the kitchen and on into the pantry, and there you’ll find cakes, ham, beef, cold chicken, roast pig, apple-dumplings, and anything else your heart desires.”

The wolf needed no second invitation. That same night he went to the house, squeezed through the drain into the kitchen and then the pantry, and ate and drank there until he was full. When he had had enough he wanted to leave, but he had stuffed himself so much that he could not fit out the way he had come in.

This was exactly what Tom had been counting on. He started shouting at the top of his voice, making as much noise as he could. “Will you be quiet?” said the wolf. “You’ll wake everyone in the house with all this racket.” “What do I care?” said the little man. “You’ve had your fun, and now I feel like enjoying myself.” And he began to sing and shout as loudly as he could.

The woodman and his wife woke at the noise and peeked through a crack in the door. When they saw a wolf in there, you can imagine how badly they were frightened. The woodman ran for his axe and handed his wife a scythe. “You stay back,” said the woodman, “and when I’ve struck him on the head, you must slash him open with the scythe.” Tom heard every word and cried out, “Father, father! I’m here, the wolf has swallowed me.” “Heaven be praised!” said his father. “We’ve found our dear child again.” He told his wife not to use the scythe, in case she hurt the boy. Then he swung hard, hit the wolf on the head, and killed him on the spot. When the wolf was dead they cut open his body and set Tommy free. “Ah,” said the father, “how afraid we have been for you!” “Yes, father,” he answered, “I think I’ve traveled all over the world, one way or another, since we parted, and now I’m very glad to be home and breathing fresh air again.” “Why, where have you been?” asked his father. “I’ve been in a mouse-hole—and in a snail-shell—and down a cow’s throat—and in the wolf’s belly. And yet here I am again, safe and sound.”
“Well,” they said, “you’re back now, and we will never sell you again, not for all the riches in the world.”

Then they hugged and kissed their dear little son and gave him plenty to eat and drink, because he was very hungry. They fetched him new clothes as well, since his old ones had been ruined on his journey. So Master Thumb stayed at home in peace with his father and mother. He had been a great traveler and had done and seen many fine things, and he liked telling the whole story, but he always agreed that, after all, there’s no place like HOME!
